'''''Bromus madritensis''''' is a species of [[Bromus|brome grass]] known by the common name '''compact brome'''.<ref name="PLANTS"/> The [[Botanical name#Components of plant names|specific epithet]] ''madritensis'' refers to [[Madrid]], [[Spain]]. It has a [[diploid number]] of 28.

There are two subspecies:
*''Bromus madritensis'' subsp. ''madritensis'': panicles less dense, stem and leaf sheath less hairy
*''Bromus madritensis'' subsp. ''rubens'' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Bromus rubens'') – '''foxtail brome''', '''foxtail chess''', '''red brome''': dense panicles and slightly hairy stems

==Description==
[[File:Bromus madritensis rubens in desert.jpg|thumb|left|Reddish subspecies ''rubens'' habit]]

''Bromus madritensis'' is a winter annual grass, growing solitary or tufted, with erect or ascending [[Culm (botany)|culm]]s growing {{convert|20-70|cm|abbr=on}} high. The leaf sheaths are downy or slightly hairy. The grass lacks [[Auricle (botany)|auricle]]s and the glabrous [[ligule]]s are {{convert|1.5-2|mm|abbr=on}} long. Its flat leaf blades are either glabrous or slightly hairy, and measure {{convert|4-20|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1-5|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The erect and ellipsoid [[panicle]]s are {{convert|3-12|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2-6|cm|abbr=on}} wide, with short branches that ascend and slightly spread. The branches never droop and bear one or two [[spikelet]]s each. The spikelets are {{convert|4-6|cm|abbr=on}} long, longer than the panicle branches, and bear seven to eleven [[floret]]s. The spikelets vary in color from green to distinctly purplish-red. The lightly hairy [[glume]]s taper at their ends and have translucent margins. The lower glumes are one-nerved and {{convert|5-10|mm|abbr=on}} long, and the upper glumes are three-nerved and {{convert|10-15|mm|abbr=on}} long. The glabrous and slightly rough [[Lemma (botany)|lemma]]s are {{convert|1.5-2|cm|abbr=on}} long. The lemmas are hairier towards their edges and have five to seven veins. The [[Awn (botany)|awn]]s are about the same length, {{convert|1.2-2.3|cm|abbr=on}} long, and curve slightly. The [[anther]]s are {{convert|0.5-1|mm|abbr=on}} long. The [[caryopsis|caryopses]] are as long as {{convert|11|mm|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Manual>{{cite book |title=Gray's Manual of Botany |author= Merrit Lyndon Fernald |year= 1970 |editor= R. C. Rollins |publisher= D. Van Nostrand Company |edition= Eighth (Centennial) – Illustrated|isbn= 0-442-22250-5 |page= 103}}</ref><ref name=Flora>{{cite book |title= Flora of North America: North of Mexico |volume= 24 |author= Flora of North America Editorial Committee |publisher= Oxford University Press |year= 1993 |isbn= 9780195310719 |page= 226}}</ref>

The grass emerges in early winter and remains dormant until spring when heavy rainfall and higher temperatures stimulate growth. Plants flower from this period typically until May when [[water stress]] inhibits the grass. Populations grow during periods of heavy rainfall and populations can be wiped out during extended periods of drought.<ref name=Invasive>{{cite book |title= Invasive Plants of California's Wildlands |url= https://archive.org/details/invasiveplantsof00carl |url-access= registration |editor1=Carla C. Bossard |editor2=John M. Randall |editor3=Marc C. Hoshovsky |edition= illustrated |publisher= University of California Press |year= 2000 |isbn= 9780520225473 |page= [https://archive.org/details/invasiveplantsof00carl/page/74 74-75]}}</ref>

The grass alters soil conditions and the [[Competition (biology)|competition]] brought about by the grass both negatively affect native plant populations, and the highly flammable nature of the grass produces wildfires in North American communities where fire was previously rare. Dry [[floret]]s of the weed entangle themselves in animal hair and can tear at the [[digestive tract]]s of foraging livestock.<ref name=Invasive/>

==Habitat and distribution==

''Bromus madritensis'' is native to southern and western [[Europe]] but has been introduced and naturalized nearly worldwide. In [[North America]] it is found primarily in the western [[United States]], in [[Oregon]], [[California]], and [[Arizona]]. The grass was brought to North America in 1848 and was naturalized by the 1890s.

In its native range the grass grows in cultivated fields and [[steppe]]s, and in North America it grows in waste areas, road verges, and disturbed areas, in both ranges primarily on dry stony or sandy soil.<ref name=Flora/> In California, the weedy grass occurs in areas disturbed by [[wildfire]]s. It grows from sea level to elevations of {{convert|1300|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Invasive/>
